org.hero.title: Run a Coding Jam in your city.
org.hero.lede: Hosting a Coding Jam is one of the best ways to connect the builders in your community — a room of developers leaves with a working app, a new collaborator, and someone to text the next time they get stuck. Bring the room; the kit brings the rest.
org.hero.lede.strong: From planning to execution in 2 weeks.

org.preflight.t48: Pin the checklist in the RSVP email
org.preflight.doors: Undecided? Send them to the tool picker
tools.title: Two tools. Two very different afternoons.
tools.lede: Neither is the beginner option. It comes down to what's already on your laptop, and whether you want a desktop IDE at all. Four questions, then bring the one that fits.
tools.known: Already know which one you want?
tools.setupCta: Set it up for your jam →
tools.q1.q: What's on the laptop you'll bring?
tools.q1.a1: A browser. That's how I like to work.
tools.q1.a2: An editor, a terminal and Git — all set up and in use.
tools.q2.q: Antigravity is a desktop IDE. Where do you stand?
tools.q2.a1: I'd rather not install anything — browser only, please.
tools.q2.a2: Already have it, or happy to install it before the jam.
tools.q3.q: Building the thing itself — what sounds better?
tools.q3.a1: Describe what I want, then shape what comes back.
tools.q3.a2: Keep my own project and let the agent edit files in it.
tools.q4.q: What do you want to walk out with?
tools.q4.a1: Something live I can send people a link to.
tools.q4.a2: A repo on my machine I can keep building on.
tools.aiStudio.blurb: Nothing to install, nothing to break on the night. You describe what you want and shape what comes back.
tools.antigravity.verdict: Bring the laptop you already work on.
tools.antigravity.blurb: An AI-driven IDE on your own machine. Your editor, your terminal, your repo — with the agent doing the typing.
sched.title: Two hours. Four movements.
sched.lede: We keep the talking short and the building long. Organizers facilitate; the room creates. This shape repeats across every track — it's the muscle memory.
sched.note: Most of the two hours is Build, and it's deliberately loose — the agent does the typing, participants decide what it's making. The codelab is there for anyone who wants a structured route through it, not a script the room has to follow.
sched.protip.label: Pro tip
sched.protip: Pre-warm the deploy target by pushing a hello-world before doors open. The first deploy of the night is usually the slowest.
sched.watch.label: Watch out
sched.watch: Your demo is your most important deliverable. Practice it once on the morning of, with the actual production stack you'll use on stage.
tl.intro.title: Intro
tl.intro.body:
Grab a name tag and a slice, say hello to the instructor, and meet the people either side of you — you'll be asking them things later, so it pays to know their names now. Low pressure, high creativity, ship something messy.

Then a quick word on what the room is building tonight, and you're off.
tl.setup.title: Credits & setup
tl.setup.body: The instructor shares the Google Cloud credits with the room. Everyone gets their environment ready — whichever tool they brought. Nobody should be installing anything once the build starts.
tl.build.title: Build
tl.build.body:
Heads down, and enjoy it — this is the part everyone came for. The agent does the typing; you decide what it's making. Ask the room when you get stuck; someone two seats away hit the same wall ten minutes ago.

Want more structure? The codelab walks the spec-driven route — Setup → Plan → Review → Build → API → Verify — but nobody has to follow it.
tl.share.title: Share & submit
tl.share.body:
Show the room what you made — two minutes, screen-shared from your seat. Half-finished is welcome; the wobbly ones are usually the most interesting. Say what surprised you along the way, and cheer for everyone else while you're at it.

Then submit your build before you leave. This is the one thing not to skip — it's what puts your name and your chapter on the showcase, and it takes about two minutes.
org.skip.title: Get every build submitted before people leave.
org.skip.lede: Two minutes per person, in the room. Once everyone walks out, it never happens.
org.checklist.ag.title: Antigravity checklist
org.checklist.ag.body: Antigravity, Git and a Gemini API key — plus uv, Node and disk-space extras. For anyone bringing a laptop they already code on.
org.checklist.ai.title: AI Studio checklist
org.checklist.ai.body: A browser and a Google account. For everyone who'd rather not install anything — which is a preference, not a limitation.
org.credits.title: Optional: GCP project + Google Cloud credits
org.credits.body: Your job, not theirs. Recommended when running an official GDG event — Google Cloud credits cover API spend and tie to the chapter KPI. Note they only apply to the Antigravity path, which bills through a Cloud project; anyone on AI Studio uses its free tier and needs nothing from you. Skip this entirely for casual jams.
org.credits.ask: for credits. Send a date, a headcount and your GCP project ID.
org.credits.emailBlurb: Send once people have RSVPed. Points them at the right setup guide.
org.present.title: Present, then submit.
org.present.lede: Rooms reliably do the first and forget the second. Put both on the schedule.
org.present.alt: Participants presenting their builds at the end of a jam.
org.present.s1.title: Get people presenting
org.present.s1.lede: Three volunteers. Two minutes each. From their seat.
org.present.s1.r1: Ask at the halfway mark, not the end
org.present.s1.r2: Pick a half-broken one on purpose
org.present.s1.r3: Ask each one: what surprised you?
org.present.s2.title: Then everyone submits
org.present.s2.lede: Not just the presenters. In the room, before anyone packs up.
org.present.s2.r1: Put the submit link on the projector
org.present.s2.r2: Say out loud that half-finished is fine
org.present.s2.r3: Screenshot required; repo and demo optional
org.signs.g1: Participants can say in one line what they set out to build
org.signs.g2: Someone says 'wait, that's a polished-version feature' mid-build
org.signs.g3: Drop-ins are scoping their own build without being walked through it
org.signs.g4: At the end, the variations between participants are wide
org.signs.b1: Participants copy the demo verbatim instead of making it theirs
org.signs.b2: Builds keep slipping past 45 minutes because everyone added more features
org.signs.b3: At Compare Notes, every project looks the same
org.signs.b4: Wall of Vibes stays empty halfway through
org.signs.reset: When you see the latter: pause, get them to say out loud what they are building, and re-read the question this track emphasizes. The reset usually re-anchors the room.
org.faq.lede: Four issues that come up in almost every room. If a participant is stuck for more than 5 minutes, check these first.
org.cta.title: Got everything you need?
org.cta.body: Open a track, grab the kit, and start preparing. Once you've hosted, share what your room shipped on the showcase — it helps other GDGs get started.
track.onlyRule: That is the only rule. What you build inside it is yours to imagine — there is no spec to follow and no right answer. Bring the idea you have been sitting on, or invent one in the room. The best builds are the ones nobody saw coming.
track.followBrief: Follow the brief and the starter repo. The scope is fixed so it ships inside the build block.
track.optionalExamples: Optional. These are examples, not a menu — the point of this track is that you choose.

faq.c1.title: GCP credits not linked
faq.c1.sym: Gemini API call returns 403 / quota error halfway through Verify.
faq.c1.fix: During Setup, link the Google Cloud credits to the GCP project at console.cloud.google.com/billing. If you skipped GCP entirely, AI Studio works for free in the browser — send them there instead.
faq.c2.title: API key not in .env
faq.c2.sym: App loads but every Gemini call returns 401.
faq.c2.fix: Open the project root, confirm `.env` exists (NOT `.env.example`), and the key is `GEMINI_API_KEY=...` with no quotes around the value. Restart the dev server after editing.
faq.c3.title: Antigravity on Apple Silicon
faq.c3.sym: App opens but the agent panel hangs on first prompt.
faq.c3.fix: Make sure you downloaded the arm64 build, not Intel. Quit the app fully (Cmd-Q, not just close window) and reopen. If still stuck, check Activity Monitor that the process is `Apple` architecture.
faq.c4.title: uv vs pip confusion
faq.c4.sym: Participant runs `pip install`, gets ModuleNotFoundError later.
faq.c4.fix: The codelab uses uv. Direct them to `uv sync` (installs deps from pyproject.toml) and `uv run <command>` (replaces `python <command>`). pip will silently install into the wrong environment.
notes.title: What to say, what to watch, what to fish for.
notes.lede: You do not demo anything. Whatever you show becomes the room's default, which turns an open track into a prescribed one. Read the requirement, let people choose, and spend the session watching for the one failure mode each track produces.
notes.ifAsked: If someone asks what to build

submit.fromJam.body: Open your jam’s page and use the submit link there. Your build is credited to that jam automatically, and you skip picking it from a list.
submit.great.1: Even half-finished. A clickable demo beats a clean README every time.
submit.great.2: 1-2 sentences on what you didn’t expect. Other builders learn from this most.
submit.great.3: 2-4 sentences on what your project does and who it’s for. Helps people decide what to click on.

submit.heads.privacy: Sign-in is via Google. Your name and avatar appear publicly with the build; your email is stored privately for moderation only.
submit.why.body: It keeps the showcase real — no spam bots, no impersonation, accurate attribution to the GDG that shipped the work.

submit.gate.body: Submissions are tied to a real Google identity so the showcase stays free of spam and credit goes to the person who actually built the thing. Your name and avatar appear publicly with the build; your email is kept private and used only for moderation.
submit.gate.p1: One-click sign-in — no new password to remember.
submit.gate.p2: Avatar from your Google profile appears on your build card.
submit.gate.p3: Your email stays private — never displayed.
submit.gate.p4: You can sign out any time from the top nav.

myjams.title: Your jams.
myjams.lede: Each jam is one event with one topic. Pick a built-in track, point at your own materials, write a topic from scratch, or leave it open — then share the link with your room.
myjams.empty.title: No jams yet.
myjams.empty.body: Create your first one and you’ll get a shareable page with the topic, the schedule, and a submission link for everything your room ships.

notorg.title: Organizer access needed.
notorg.body: Jam pages are published by organizers on the roster. If you’re running a Coding Jam for your chapter, ask an admin to add your Google account and this page will open up.
about.lede: GDG Coding Jams transform standard tech meetups into vibrant, hands-on community sandboxes where developers actually build together. Two hours, a slice of pizza, Google’s AI stack — and a real prototype walking out the door.
about.why.title: A jam, not a hackathon.
about.why.p1: Think of a musical jam or an after-work pottery class. Instruments out, a creative prompt, two hours of making something tangible alongside friends. We bring that energy to software.
about.why.p2: No sit-and-listen tech talks. No 48-hour competitive hackathon grind. Just blueprints, tech access, and collaborative space.
about.value1.title: Frictionless upskilling
about.value1.body: Developers learn Google's AI tools best when they're actively building. We remove the blank-page syndrome.
about.value2.title: Low organizer burden
about.value2.body: Materials, timelines, and goals provided. Organizers book a room and bring the snacks.
about.value3.title: Stronger communities
about.value3.body: Collaborative problem-solving builds a deeper network than passive networking ever does.
about.rhythm.title: Two hours, four movements.
about.rhythm.body: Predictable, fast-paced, engaging. We keep the talking short and the building long. Organizers act as facilitators, guiding the room through a unified creative process.
about.goal.a: The goal in the room is always to ship the
about.goal.c: — the one thing that proves the concept. Push toward the polished version on your own time.
about.topic.title: Set your own topic. Or borrow a built-in one.
about.topic.p1: The organizer running the room decides what it builds. Point at your own dataset, take on something your city actually needs, or write a brief from scratch — the format holds either way, because the two hours are what make it a jam, not the subject.
about.topic.p2: Borrow a built-in topic instead. Most of them set one requirement — build an Android app, put it on a map, make it multiplayer — and leave what to build to each participant, so the room shares a constraint rather than a spec. Two are complete, drop-in projects with a brief and a starter repo already written, for a room that would rather follow along.
about.topic.p3: None of them depend on each other. Pick whichever sounds most fun for your community and go.
about.differ.1: — one requirement, everyone picks their own build
about.differ.2: — a written brief and a starter repo to follow
about.differ.3: — write a brief from scratch, or bring a dataset
about.cta2.title: Ready to jam?
about.cta2.body: Open any track and ship a working app in the next 45 minutes. Or grab the kit and host a jam in your city.
hiw.title: Four beats, and you’re out with a working app.
hiw.lede: No prep required. No prior project. Drop in to any track on any week.
hiw.1.title: Show up
hiw.1.body: Bring a laptop. No prep, no prior project. The room handles the rest.
hiw.2.title: Pick a topic
hiw.2.body: Your chapter has one for the week, or you bring your own idea. Two minutes of deciding what you're making.
hiw.3.title: Build together
hiw.3.body: AI does the typing; you direct it. Everyone's building at once, so the person next to you is the fastest way past a wall.
hiw.4.title: Share what you made
hiw.4.body: Two minutes each, screen-shared from your seat. Then it goes on the showcase — half-finished is welcome.
guide.before.title: A pre-flight checklist.
guide.before.body: Do this at home, on decent wifi. Half the workshop time is otherwise lost to setup — this gives it back. Turning up without it is still fine; pair with a TA.
guide.walkthrough.title: What you’ll do, step by step.
guide.notSure.body: The two tools suit different rooms. If this one doesn’t sound like you, the other probably does.
guide.running.body: Put whichever tool you’ve chosen in the event description, so people arrive with it ready instead of installing during the session.
ais.tagline: Open a tab, describe what you want, watch it appear. Nothing to install before the doors open.
ais.forWhom: For builders who don't write code day to day — designers, PMs, students, anyone with an idea and a browser.
ais.notice.heading: The Google Cloud credits aren't for this path — and you don't need them.
ais.notice.p1: The credits your organizer hands out attach to a Google Cloud billing account, which is the Antigravity path. AI Studio doesn’t touch any of that: sign in with your Google account and start building. Nothing to claim, nothing to bill, nothing to configure.
ais.notice.p2: It’s free but not unlimited — if you push it hard you may be asked to slow down for a moment. Wait it out rather than starting over; you won’t lose anything.
ais.notice.p3: Need heavier or longer-running usage than that? Switch to the Antigravity path, where the credits do apply.
ais.install.1.title: A browser
ais.install.1.body: Anything modern. AI Studio runs entirely in the tab — there's no IDE to download, no package manager, no terminal.
ais.install.2.title: A Google account
ais.install.2.body: Sign in at aistudio.google.com and you're in — no key, no project, no setup. Use the same account you'll share your build with afterwards.
ais.worth.note: Optional, but it makes the session smoother.
ais.worth.1.title: Your inputs, ready to go
ais.worth.1.body: If your track needs a photo, a dataset or a block of text, have it on the machine before you sit down rather than hunting for it mid-build.
ais.step1.title: Sign in
ais.step1.body: Open AI Studio with your Google account. That's the whole setup — no workspace to create, no key to generate, nothing to claim.
ais.step2.title: Hit + App in the sidebar
ais.step2.body: That's it, that's the step. Everything you build lives in there — no project scaffolding, no install, no terminal. Describe what you want and start.
ais.step2.alt: The + App button in the AI Studio sidebar
ais.step3.title: Shape the result
ais.step3.body: The first version is never the one you keep — that's the point of working this way. Narrow it down: change the tone, fix the layout, drop the feature that isn't earning its place. Small, specific asks beat one long one.
ais.step4.title: Get a link you can share
ais.step4.body: How to get from a working prototype to something you can send people — and onto the showcase.
ag.tagline: Your editor, your terminal, your repo — with the agent doing the typing.
ag.forWhom: For people who already write code and have a working dev setup on the laptop they're bringing.
ag.codelab.heading: Follow the codelab.
ag.codelab.blurb: Zero to a working app in about an hour, one step at a time. It walks you through Setup, Plan, Review, Build, API and Verify — you direct the agent, it does the typing.
ag.install.note: Required — the session assumes all three are working.
ag.install.1.body: The Jam runs on Antigravity — without it you can't follow the codelab. It's a sizeable download, so do it before the day rather than on venue wifi.
ag.install.2.title: Git, and a GitHub account
ag.install.2.body: Every starter is a GitHub repo you clone during setup. Check you can actually clone something — an unconfigured SSH key is the classic five-minutes-lost moment.
ag.install.3.title: A Google account, for the Gemini API
ag.install.3.body: You'll create an API key at ai.google.dev. The free tier covers a two-hour session comfortably. Use the same account you'll share your build with afterwards.
ag.worth.note: Not required on the day — the codelab covers uv, and the rest just smooth things out.
ag.worth.1.body: The Python package manager the starters use — it replaces pip and venv, and installs the right Python for you if you haven't got one. The codelab walks you through it, so you can also leave this until the day.
ag.worth.2.title: Node.js 20+ and npm
ag.worth.2.body: Not needed for the Python backend, but the frontend-heavy tracks are easier with it, and most JS tooling assumes it. Check with node -v — if that prints a version you're already set.
ag.worth.3.title: A terminal you're comfortable in
ag.worth.3.body: You'll run a handful of commands. Whatever you already use is the right one — the jam doesn't care which shell.
ag.worth.4.title: Room on disk
ag.worth.4.body: A couple of GB free for the IDE and its dependencies. Worth checking before the day rather than discovering it mid-install.
ag.step1.title: Claim your credits
ag.step1.body: Your instructor shares the claim link on the day — it isn't public. Open it with your Gmail account, not a work or school one: the credits attach to whichever Google identity you claim with, and a managed account often can't accept them. If you haven't joined the Google Developer Program before, it'll ask you to join first. That's free and takes a minute.
ag.step1.alt: Claiming the credits, including the Join the Google Developer Program prompt
ag.step2.title: Create a Google Cloud project and attach billing
ag.step2.body: Make a fresh project for the jam rather than reusing one — it keeps the credits, quotas and any mess separate from whatever else you run. Then attach the billing account your credits landed in, or nothing you do next will bill against them.
ag.step2.alt: Creating the project, then attaching the billing account
ag.step3.title: Enable Agent Platform
ag.step3.body: Open Agent Platform on your new project and hit Enable at the top of the page. Nothing downstream works until this is on, and it's the step that most often gets skipped.
ag.step3.alt: Hitting Enable at the top of the Agent Platform overview
ag.step4.title: Copy your project ID
ag.step4.body: The project ID, not the display name — they're usually different, and only the ID works. You'll paste it into Antigravity in a moment.
ag.step4.alt: Copying the project ID from the Cloud Console
ag.step5.title: Open Antigravity — sign in with Google Cloud
ag.step5.body: This is the step people miss. On the welcome screen, choose the Google Cloud project option rather than your personal Google account, so the session runs against the project your credits are in.
ag.step5.alt: Choosing Google Cloud project on the Antigravity welcome screen
ag.step6.title: Paste your project ID
ag.step6.body: Paste the ID you copied in step 4. Antigravity connects to that project, and you're ready to build.
ag.step6.alt: Pasting the project ID into Antigravity

me.publicTitle: Public profile — share this link with anyone.
me.badges.title: Collect them as you ship.
me.badges.body: Every build counts — including ones where you’re credited as a collaborator. Each milestone unlocks a Google badge you can claim and add to your profile.
me.badges.gdp.a: The badges you earn here also show up on your
me.badges.gdp.b: — same Google account you signed in with.
me.builds.emptyBody: Ship your first jam build to unlock your Builder badge.
sc.lede: Real builds from real GDG chapters. Two hours, one pizza, one prototype. Search by name, narrow to a GDG group or a date range — or scroll until something makes you want to fork it.
sc.empty.filteredBody: Try a different name, group, or date range.
sc.empty.noneBody: Be the first to ship one — your GDG could go on the hero board.
cp.1.title: Setup
cp.1.body: Install Antigravity, clone the starter, init the environment.
cp.2.title: Plan
cp.2.body: Spec conversation generates three docs: PRD, UI/UX, engineering + tests.
cp.3.title: Review
cp.3.body: Read the docs. Leave inline comments. Iterate until approved.
cp.4.title: Build
cp.4.body: Antigravity generates the app and tests. Auto-fix loop on failures.
cp.5.title: API
cp.5.body: Create the GCP project, link credits, get the Gemini API key, fill .env.
cp.6.title: Verify
cp.6.body: Run the dev server. Click through. Fix the doc, not the code.
banned.title: Your account is banned.
banned.p1: This Google account has been suspended from GDG Coding Jams for violating the submission rules, and any projects submitted from it have been removed.
banned.p2: This sign-in attempt has been logged and reported to the jam organizers, who can see the reason for the suspension along with every attempt to sign in since it was applied. You will not be able to sign in or submit a project.
banned.p3: If you believe this was a mistake, reply to the organizers through your GDG chapter — a suspension can be lifted by an admin.
nf.title: Off the lineup.
nf.body: We couldn’t find that page. Try one of the jams instead.
tb.ships.title: The version everyone leaves with.
tb.while.title: Things worth deciding early.
tb.polished.title: What the at-home build adds.
org.credits.a: Your job, not theirs. Recommended when running an official GDG event — Google Cloud credits cover API spend and tie to the chapter KPI. Note they only apply to the
org.credits.b: , which bills through a Cloud project; anyone on AI Studio uses its free tier and needs nothing from you. Skip this entirely for casual jams.
newjam.copyFrom.b: is filled in below — the topic, your chapter, the links. Set a new date, adjust whatever changed, and this saves as a separate jam with its own page. The original is untouched.
newjam.draftFirst: It saves as a draft first — nothing is public until you set it to Published.
email.bodyLabel: Body — edit anything in square brackets before sending
asst.title: Set it up by chatting.
asst.lede: A few questions — your chapter, what the room is building, when it runs — and the form fills itself in. Ask anything about the tracks along the way. You still review it and press Create.
asst.creates: Creates the jam — you choose if it goes live
meta.site.title: GDG Coding Jams — Build with AI. Together. In two hours.
meta.site.desc: Turnkey 2-hour AI build sessions for GDG communities. Show up, grab pizza, ship a real prototype with Google's AI tools.
meta.aiStudio.title: Set up Google AI Studio for your jam — GDG Coding Jams
meta.aiStudio.desc: Everything in the browser. No install, no terminal — the setup guide for builders bringing AI Studio to a Coding Jam.
meta.antigravity.title: Install Antigravity and set it up for your jam — GDG Coding Jams
meta.antigravity.desc: An AI-driven IDE on your own machine. The pre-flight checklist and setup guide for builders bringing Antigravity to a Coding Jam.
meta.jams.title: Jams — GDG Coding Jams
meta.jams.desc: Coding Jams happening around the world. Each one is run by a GDG organizer with their own topic for the week.
meta.banned.title: Account suspended
meta.try.title: Build a jam page — GDG Coding Jams
meta.try.desc: Put together a Coding Jam page in two minutes. No account needed.
meta.track.title: {name} — Coding Jam track
meta.jam.title: {title} — Coding Jam
meta.profile.title: {name} — GDG Coding Jams
meta.profile.descOne: {name} shipped {project} at a Coding Jam with {chapter}.
meta.profile.descMany: {name} has shipped {n} builds at Coding Jams with {chapter}.
jfm.kind.track.blurb: Use one of the built-in topics. Nothing to write — your page pulls the requirement, guidance and codelab. Most topics set one rule and let each person choose what to build; "Build your own idea" sets none at all.
jfm.kind.custom.blurb: Bring your own codelab or dataset, write a topic from scratch, or both. Only the title and tagline are required — fill in as much of the rest as you want.
jfm.stillDraft: Still a draft — set it to Published when you’re ready to share the link.
jfm.name: Jam name
jfm.name.hint: What you'd put on the meetup listing.
jfm.url.hintNew: Assigned when you save — a short link you can read out to the room.
jfm.url.hint: Short enough to put on a slide. This is the link to share.
jfm.date.hint: Optional — leave blank if you haven't picked one.
jfm.rsvp.hint: Optional. Your Meetup or Luma page.
jfm.whichTopic.hint: Your jam page shows this track's brief, codelab and demo. Track 09 is the open one — no set topic, everyone brings their own idea.
jfm.tagline.hint: One line the room can read off the projector.
jfm.mmv.hint: Optional — but it's the field that keeps a room on scope. The smallest version that still works, and what you're explicitly not building.
jfm.thinkAbout.hint: Optional. Up to {n} prompts to keep builders on scope.
jfm.tech.hint: Optional. Up to {n} short labels — what they'll actually touch.
jfm.polished.hint: Optional. Up to {n} ideas for the at-home build.
jfm.hero.hint: Optional. Shown at the top of your jam page. PNG, JPEG, WebP or GIF, up to 8 MiB — it uploads when you save.
jfm.links.note: All optional. If you're bringing an existing codelab or dataset, this is the only section you need.
jfm.status.hint: Drafts are only visible to you. Published jams appear on /jams and anyone with the link can see them.
jfm.status.archived: Archived — hidden, kept for the record
try.title: Build a jam page in two minutes.
try.lede: Fill this in and you get a shareable link — no sign-in, nothing saved on our side. The whole page travels inside the link itself, so keep it somewhere safe: lose the link and the page is gone.
try.upsell.a: Want a short URL, an image, and a place for builders to submit what they made?
try.linksHint: All optional. Must start with https://
try.whichTopic.hint: Most topics set one requirement and let each person choose what to build.
try.mmv.hint: Optional. Keeps the room on scope.
try.unsaved.body: It lives entirely in this link — copy it before you close the tab.
try.permanent.body: A published jam gets a short URL, a hero image, and a submission page where your room shares what they built — all credited to you.
try.yourLink.body: This is the whole page. Anyone you send it to sees exactly what you see.
sf.fromJamInline: Submitting for a jam? Open its page and submit from there instead —
jam.submit.title: Built something at this jam?
jam.submit.body: Put it on the showcase. It takes two minutes, half-finished is welcome, and your build is credited to this jam automatically.
org.signup.label: I want to be an organizer
org.signup.title: Ask for organizer access
org.signup.blurb: Tell the Google Community Ambassadors team which GDG chapter you organize, or link your GDE profile. Fill in the bracketed lines, and send it from the Google account you will sign in with.
org.signup.note: Publishing a jam page needs a spot on the organizer roster. Not on it yet? Ask above — it takes one email.
email.noApp: This opens a draft in your own email app — nothing is sent from this site, and you can edit it before sending. No email app set up? Use the Copy buttons above and paste the address, subject and body into Gmail or whichever webmail you use.
